content: Interruptions in tuberculosis (TB) treatment during incarceration or when individuals are transferred between facilities can be mitigated by linking them to community-based care upon release. Systematic TB screening should be prioritized for all prisoners and prison staff, regardless of their HIV status, in settings with high TB prevalence in the general or prison population, high incarceration rates, significant HIV or multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) prevalence, or poor living conditions in detention facilities. Screening should occur upon entry into the facility, with annual follow-ups if resources allow. Efforts to improve living conditions, reduce overcrowding, provide supplementary nutrition, and control infection transmission are critical. All detention facilities should implement infection-control plans that include policies to enhance ventilation, increase access to natural light, and separate prisoners with infectious TB from others, particularly those living with HIV. Similarly, individuals suspected of having MDR-TB should be isolated from other prisoners, including those with drug-sensitive TB. Access to prevention, screening, diagnosis, and treatment services must align with medical ethics, national standards, and established guidelines. These interventions should prioritize the best interests of the patient, ensuring that all services are voluntary, provided with informed consent, confidential, non-discriminatory, and respectful. Integrating collaborative TB and HIV services into a comprehensive care package for people who inject drugs is essential for addressing these overlapping health challenges effectively.
